analysis.one_liner: Requires police to get a judge's warrant before searching data stored in your car.
analysis.headline: The bill would have required a warrant before police searched a car's onboard data, but it never left the House Judiciary Committee and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern cars record where you went, what you said inside the cabin, camera footage, and diagnostics. The bill would have made it illegal for police to pull that data without a warrant from a judge, with narrow exceptions if you consent or in an emergency. Evidence gathered illegally would have been thrown out of court. The bill was introduced with support from one Democrat and one Republican, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Every driver and passenger. Cars today are rolling data recorders — navigation history, event data from crashes, images from onboard cameras, and communications to and from occupants. Under current practice, police can often reach this data without a judge's approval. The bill would have given drivers the same basic protection for their car's data that the Constitution's warrant requirement is meant to provide for phones and homes, and it would have suppressed any evidence police collected in violation.

how_it_helps.text: Would prohibit any federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement officer from accessing onboard and telematics data in a noncommercial vehicle — navigation data, diagnostics, entertainment system data, images from onboard sensors or cameras, and communications to and from occupants — unless they first obtain a warrant from a judge.

Would make vehicle data seized in violation of the ban inadmissible in any trial, hearing, grand jury, or other proceeding, and would bar evidence derived from it — so an illegal search would actually cost investigators the evidence.

Would tightly constrain the consent loophole: consent would have to be voluntary and informed, in writing or recorded, specific about what data and time period is covered, and a passenger 14 or older could object to the search. A generic click-through privacy policy would not count as consent.

Would allow warrantless access only in a genuine emergency involving immediate danger of death or serious injury, and even then police would have to ask a court to approve the search within 48 hours — if the court says no, the data could not be used.

analysis.who_pays: Police departments and prosecutors would lose the ability to pull a car's stored data on their own authority. They would need to get a warrant, as they already must for phone records and home searches. In investigations where speed mattered and the emergency exception did not apply, some evidence might arrive later or be lost, and some cases could be harder to prove.

drawbacks.text: The bill would add friction to real investigations. Officers would need a judge's warrant to access data that today they can sometimes pull directly — for example, navigation history or crash data — which could slow cases where there was no emergency but time still mattered.

The consent rules are unusually strict: written (or recorded) consent, a stated scope and time period, an explanation that consent is optional, and a veto for any passenger 14 or older. That protects drivers, but it would also make routine, voluntary cooperation between citizens and police harder to document and use.

The exclusionary rule cuts both ways. If data is gathered in violation, it and everything derived from it is barred from every proceeding — including state courts — which means genuinely guilty defendants could walk when the violation happens.

The protection has holes: data covered by the foreign-intelligence surveillance laws is excluded, and data collected from outside the vehicle — including speed and geolocation data gathered for traffic, law enforcement, or toll collection — is not covered at all, so a common way of tracking a car's movements would remain outside the warrant requirement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and growing: cars now store the kind of intimate record that phones did a decade ago, and the bill would simply extend the ordinary warrant rule to them, with a workable emergency exception. The costs are modest and familiar — investigations run through the warrant process, and evidence from violations is suppressed, which is the standard price of enforcing search protections. The bill's blind spots (FISA, and tracking data collected from outside the car) keep it from being comprehensive, but on balance it is a straightforward privacy safeguard whose main flaw is that it never went anywhere.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee until the Congress ended — no committee vote, no floor vote, ever.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna, a Democrat, introduced the bill on November 17, 2021, joined by Republican Rep. Peter Meijer as its only cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; the committee never took it up.

On November 1, 2022 — two months before the Congress expired — the bill was referred to the subcommittee on crime, terrorism, and homeland security, its last recorded action. It died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police and prosecutors keep the ability to access a car's stored data without a judge's warrant. No one else's situation changed, because the bill never became law.

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require warrants for searching car data.

for.name: Peter Meijer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only other original supporter.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in his committee for its entire life; no markup or committee vote was ever scheduled, and it was sent to a subcommittee two months before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a bipartisan pair of sponsors — one Democrat and one Republican — but with only two supporters and no votes ever taken, no partisan pattern can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped police of the ability to pull navigation, sensor, camera, and communications data from cars without a judge's warrant, and would have suppressed evidence gathered that way. In this bill, the interests of law enforcement run directly against the privacy of drivers.

The bill does not limit how much data cars collect — it accepts that vehicles are data recorders and only channels government access to that data through warrants, even carving out manufacturer-installed software from the definition. The industry keeps building the surveillance, and the bill would not change what it gathers or sells.
